lesson.title: The Chips That Built the Modern World: America's Semiconductor Industry
lesson.summary: The American semiconductor industry grew from a single 1947 invention into a globalized business whose geography, dominated by Taiwan and South Korea, now sits at the center of active U.S. economic and national security policy debates.
lesson.body:
The American semiconductor industry grew out of the same 1947 invention that launched the broader Digital Revolution: the transistor, developed at Bell Labs by John Bardeen, Walter Brattain, and William Shockley. Shockley later moved to Mountain View, California, and founded Shockley Semiconductor Laboratory in 1956, hoping to commercialize transistor technology. Personality conflicts led eight of his researchers, including Robert Noyce and Gordon Moore, to leave the following year and found Fairchild Semiconductor, a company often credited with establishing the Santa Clara Valley area, later nicknamed Silicon Valley, as the center of American electronics manufacturing. In 1968, Noyce and Moore left Fairchild to found Intel, which became one of the industry's most important companies.

The integrated circuit, invented independently by Jack Kilby at Texas Instruments in 1958 and Robert Noyce at Fairchild in 1959, made it possible to place many transistors on a single chip, and the industry's growth from that point followed a remarkably consistent pattern. In 1965, Gordon Moore observed that the number of transistors that could fit on a chip of a given size was roughly doubling every year or two, a trend that became known as Moore's Law and that held, with some slowing in more recent years, for decades, driving continuous increases in computing power and continuous decreases in cost.

As with the broader Digital Revolution, government demand played a crucial early role. Cold War military needs and NASA's Apollo program during the Space Race created some of the first large scale markets for integrated circuits, since both required electronics that were lightweight, reliable, and compact. This early government demand helped semiconductor manufacturers achieve the production scale that eventually brought prices down enough for the consumer electronics markets, personal computers, and later smartphones described elsewhere in this unit, connecting the semiconductor industry to America's much longer tradition of industrial innovation stretching back to the Industrial Revolution, when new manufacturing techniques and factory systems similarly transformed the American economy and its workforce.

By the late twentieth century, semiconductor manufacturing had become increasingly globalized. Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company, founded by Morris Chang in 1987, pioneered a business model in which a company manufactures chips designed by other firms, and it grew into the world's largest and most advanced chip foundry, alongside major manufacturers like Samsung in South Korea. This left the United States, which still led in chip design, increasingly dependent on manufacturing capacity located in East Asia. A global shortage of chips during the COVID-19 pandemic, which disrupted supply chains and idled auto factories and electronics production, drew wide attention to this dependence, and concerns about supply chain security and technological competition with China led Congress to pass the CHIPS and Science Act, which President Biden signed in August 2022, providing subsidies intended to expand domestic semiconductor manufacturing. The wisdom and effectiveness of that approach remain actively debated: supporters argue it strengthens national and economic security by reducing reliance on a small number of overseas suppliers concentrated in a geopolitically sensitive region, while critics, including some free market economists, question whether government subsidies are the most efficient way to build a competitive industry and point to the high cost per job created. As of the mid-2020s, this remains an active and unresolved area of American economic and technology policy.
